trivia_fact: Shay Banon created the predecessor to Elasticsearch — called Compass — in 2004 as a recipe search engine for his wife, who was studying to be a chef. When he rewrote it from scratch in 2010, he named it Elasticsearch and open-sourced it immediately.

Elasticsearch is built on Apache Lucene, the Java search library created by Doug Cutting in 1999. Cutting later co-created Hadoop. Lucene provides the inverted index and text analysis engine; Elasticsearch adds distributed coordination, REST APIs, and JSON document storage on top.

The "Elastic" in Elasticsearch refers to its ability to scale horizontally by adding nodes — the cluster elastically grows and shrinks. Shay Banon chose the name to emphasize this distributed-first architecture, distinguishing it from single-node search solutions.

The ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) became the dominant open-source log analytics platform. The acronym emerged organically from the community — Elastic did not originally brand it. Elastic later rebranded it as the "Elastic Stack" when they added Beats (making it technically "BELK").

Elastic NV went public on the NYSE in October 2018 (ticker: ESTC), opening at $70 per share — 94% above its IPO price of $36. The company is incorporated in the Netherlands (hence "NV") despite being operationally headquartered in San Francisco.

In January 2021, Elastic changed Elasticsearch's license from Apache 2.0 to a dual SSPL/Elastic License, specifically to prevent AWS from offering it as a managed service without contributing back. This was one of the most contentious open-source license changes in history.

When Elastic changed its license, Amazon forked the last Apache 2.0 version of Elasticsearch and Kibana, creating OpenSearch and OpenSearch Dashboards in April 2021. The fork sparked debates about who truly "owns" open-source projects and the sustainability of permissive licensing.

Elasticsearch's power comes from the inverted index: instead of mapping documents to words, it maps every word to the documents containing it. This data structure, also used by web search engines, makes full-text search nearly instantaneous regardless of corpus size.

Elasticsearch is "near-real-time" rather than real-time: by default, new documents become searchable after a 1-second refresh interval. This design trades tiny latency for dramatically better indexing throughput. The refresh interval is configurable down to milliseconds for time-critical use cases.

Elasticsearch can automatically detect and create field mappings when it encounters new JSON fields — called dynamic mapping. While convenient, this "schemaless" behavior is a common source of mapping explosion bugs where careless indexing creates thousands of unwanted fields.
